title: Gradient-Free Sampling from Generative Models via Stochastic Bounded Extremum Seeking

paper.title: Gradient-Free Sampling from Generative Models via Stochastic Bounded Extremum Seeking
paper.abstract: Abstract We introduce a sampling approach for energy- and score-based generative models that requires no gradient evaluations of the model. Replacing the drift term that would normally contain the score ∇ 𝐱 ​ log ​ p θ ​ ( 𝐱 ) \nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) with a high-frequency dithered cosine of the model’s value , α ​ ω ​ cos ⁡ ( ω ​ t + k ​ log ⁡ p θ ​ ( 𝐱 ) ) \sqrt{\alpha\omega}\,\cos(\omega t+k\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})) , produces, in the high-frequency averaging limit, Langevin Markov chain Monte Carlo for energy-based models and the reverse-time SDE of score-based diffusion. We prove that trajectories of the dithered Itô SDE converge to those of the target SDE, driven by the same Brownian motion, uniformly on compact time intervals in probability, by an averaging argument that extends bounded extremum seeking (ES) to Itô processes, with an explicit O ( ω − 1 / 2 ) O(\omega^{-1/2}) mean-square rate under global bounds. The approach is not confined to smooth targets: it extends to C 1 , 1 C^{1,1} energies with discontinuous curvature (without ellipticity requirement) and to Sobolev energies whose Hessians exist only off measure zero sets; for Lipschitz energies with gradient kinks the averaged limit remains well posed; the Krylov-Röckner integrability class is the boundary of provability. The approach provides a hard a priori bound on the per-step update rate and applies to explicitly time-varying targets on finite horizons. Gradient-free pixel-space sampling is not competitive with well-tuned backpropagation-based samplers at practical evaluation budgets; the regime where the approach offers an advantage is latent-space sampling when the model is a black box and the target drifts in time. We demonstrate latent-space tracking for time-varying images on CelebA-HQ ( 256 × 256 256{\times}256 ) from limited 1D projection measurements and latent-space EBM sampling on CIFAR-10.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Modern generative models are trained, sampled, and conditioned primarily through gradients of large neural networks. Score-based diffusion ( Song et al., 2021 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song & Ermon, 2019 ) , latent diffusion ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023 ) , and energy-based models (EBMs) ( Du & Mordatch, 2019 ; Grathwohl et al., 2020 ; Du et al., 2021 ) all rely on gradients of a trained network: guidance or likelihood signals for diffusion and flow models, and the energy gradient itself for EBMs. When the model is available inside an automatic-differentiation framework this is efficient: a backward pass costs a small constant multiple of a forward pass. Our interest is in settings where even this is unavailable or insufficient. Three such regimes recur in practice. (i) : The quantity of interest is computed by a simulator ( Cranmer et al., 2020 ) , a black-box scoring function such as the round-trip self-consistency of a bidirectional diffusion rollout ( Scheinker, 2026 ) , a quantized or compiled inference engine, or a model served behind an API, so that only function values can be obtained ( Nesterov & Spokoiny, 2017 ) . (ii) : The target distribution drifts continuously, which is the operating condition of feedback-based generative reconstruction in scientific instruments, such as evolving microstructures in dynamic coherent diffraction imaging ( Scheinker & Pokharel, 2024 ) , time-varying particle accelerator beam diagnostics ( Scheinker et al., 2026 ; Scheinker, 2024 ) , and more broadly of streaming inverse problems in which each new measurement redefines the posterior. Restarting an MCMC chain at every measurement is wasteful, and running a single gradient-based chain against a drifting target has no tracking guarantee. (iii) : Sampling in the latent space of a pretrained encoder-decoder whose internals are frozen or otherwise outside the user’s autodiff graph, as in generative-prior inverse problems ( Bora et al., 2017 ) and latent-space molecular design ( Gómez-Bombarelli et al., 2018 ) . Figure 1: Bounded ES dynamics results in various samplers depending on the choice of ( 𝐟 , 𝝈 , k , α , J ) (\mathbf{f},\bm{\sigma},k,\alpha,J) , where 𝝈 ⁡ ( 𝐱 , t ) = diag ⁡ ( g 1 ​ ( 𝐱 , t ) , … , g d ​ ( 𝐱 , t ) ) \bm{\sigma}(\mathbf{x},t)=\operatorname{diag}\!\big(g_{1}(\mathbf{x},t),\dots,g_{d}(\mathbf{x},t)\big) , μ ω , i ​ ( 𝐱 , t ) = f i ​ ( 𝐱 , t ) + g i ​ ( 𝐱 , t ) ​ α ​ ω i ​ cos ⁡ ( ω i ​ t + k ​ J ​ ( 𝐱 , t ) ) \mu_{\omega,i}(\mathbf{x},t)=f_{i}(\mathbf{x},t)\;+\;g_{i}(\mathbf{x},t)\,\sqrt{\alpha\omega_{i}}\,\cos\!\big(\omega_{i}t+k\,J(\mathbf{x},t)\big) . Averaged dynamics not changed by rough energies, but the provable results are. Above C 2 C^{2} means the a.e.-equivalence class of J J contains a C 2 C^{2} function. J J can have measure zero jumps. This paper develops a single sampling procedure for all three regimes by replacing model gradients with a high-frequency dithered cosine of the model’s value. Given a function J ⁡ ( 𝐱 , t ) J(\mathbf{x},t) that can be evaluated but not differentiated by the user, consider the stochastic feedback law d x i = 2 α ​ ω i cos ( ω i t + k J ( 𝐱 , t ) ) d t + 2 d w i , i = 1 , … , d , dx_{i}\;=\;\sqrt{2}\,\sqrt{\alpha\omega_{i}}\,\cos\!\big(\omega_{i}t+k\,J(\mathbf{x},t)\big)\,dt\;+\;\sqrt{2}\,dw_{i},\qquad i=1,\ldots,d, (1) with distinct dither frequencies ω i = ω ​ r i \omega_{i}=\omega r_{i} . As ω → ∞ \omega\to\infty the trajectories of Eq. ( 1 ) converge (in the precise sense of Theorem 1 ) to those of d ​ 𝐱 ¯ = − k ​ α ​ ∇ 𝐱 ¯ J ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ , t ) ​ d ​ t + 2 ​ d ​ 𝐰 d\bar{\mathbf{x}}=-k\alpha\,\nabla_{\bar{\mathbf{x}}}J(\bar{\mathbf{x}},t)\,dt+\sqrt{2}\,d\mathbf{w} . With J = ℰ θ J=\mathcal{E}_{\theta} and k ​ α = 1 k\alpha=1 this is Langevin MCMC for the EBM p ∝ e − ℰ θ p\propto e^{-\mathcal{E}_{\theta}} ; embedded in the appropriate drift with J = log ⁡ p θ J=\log p_{\theta} it reproduces the reverse-time SDE of score-based diffusion ( Anderson, 1982 ; Song et al., 2021 ) . The gradient ∇ 𝐱 J \nabla_{\mathbf{x}}J is never computed, only evaluated once per time step, shared across all d d coordinates. Flow-matching velocity networks are score networks up to an affine map ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023 ) , so they are covered exactly as score-only diffusion models are in Sec. 3.3 , (II): through the line-integral surrogate, not directly. The dithered feedback law is bounded extremum seeking , which originated in adaptive control of analytically unknown time-varying systems ( Scheinker, 2013 ) and was generalized to discontinuous dithers in ( Scheinker & Scheinker, 2016 ) . For generative-model sampling we extend the averaging analysis to stochastic differential equations, which is the subject of Theorem 1 and its extensions, as summarized in Figure 1 . The main contributions of this paper are: Theory: We prove that multivariate stochastic bounded ES SDE converges to Langevin / reverse-time diffusion SDE, driven by the same Brownian motion, uniformly on compact time intervals in probability as the dither frequencies tend to infinity and prove convergence in distribution on path space. This is, to our knowledge, the first averaging analysis of bounded ES in the Itô setting. Under global bounds the same proof yields the quantitative mean-square rate 𝔼 ​ sup t ≤ T ‖ 𝐱 ω − 𝐱 ¯ ‖ 2 ≤ C / ω \mathbb{E}\sup_{t\leq T}\|\mathbf{x}_{\omega}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}\|^{2}\leq C/\omega , and we show that the same sampler converges on C 1 , 1 C^{1,1} energies with discontinuous curvature and on Sobolev energies whose Hessian exists only off a null set; for Lipschitz energies with gradient kinks the averaged limit remains well posed. The boundary of provability is the Krylov-Röckner class. Algorithm 1: The finite-step sampler is provided and guidance for choosing ω \omega , { r i } \{r_{i}\} , Δ ​ t \Delta t , k k , and α \alpha . Instantiations and tempering, as corollaries: Choices of ( 𝐟 , 𝝈 , k , α , J ) (\mathbf{f},\bm{\sigma},k,\alpha,J) recover gradient-free Langevin for EBMs, gradient-free reverse-SDE sampling for models with an explicit log-density, gradient-free sampling from a classifier via the EBM–classifier correspondence ( Grathwohl et al., 2020 ) , and a single-knob λ \lambda -tempering whose stationary law is p λ p^{\lambda} . Experiments mapping the operating regime: We evaluate against gradient-based (SGLD, MALA) and zeroth-order ( Roy et al., 2022 ) baselines at matched evaluation budgets, on a synthetic testbed, on latent-space EBM sampling (CIFAR-10), and on a time-varying latent tracking problem (CelebA-HQ). Scope of claims. We do not claim that gradient-free ES sampling outperforms well-tuned gradient-based Langevin samplers in pixel space on standard benchmarks; the need to resolve the dither makes the per-step / per-quality tradeoff unfavorable there (Sec. 3.2 ). The claim is a regime expansion : the same algorithm, with guarantees, operates in settings where backpropagation is unavailable.

sections.heading: 2.2 Bounded extremum seeking
sections.text: Bounded ES ( Scheinker, 2013 ; Scheinker & Scheinker, 2016 ) is a model-independent feedback law that steers a parameter vector toward the (possibly time-varying) minimizer of an unknown cost J ⁡ ( 𝐱 , t ) J(\mathbf{x},t) using only evaluations of J J . Its defining feature is the dithered cosine update of Eq. ( 1 ), with two properties that distinguish it from generic finite-difference, simultaneous-perturbation, or smoothing-based gradient estimates ( Spall, 1992 ; Nesterov & Spokoiny, 2017 ; Roy et al., 2022 ) : (i) the update rate obeys the hard a priori bound | d ​ x i / d ​ t − noise | ≤ α ​ ω i ​ | g i | |dx_{i}/dt-\text{noise}|\leq\sqrt{\alpha\omega_{i}}\,|g_{i}| regardless of the magnitude of J J , and (ii) a single scalar evaluation of J J per time instant drives all d d coordinates simultaneously, rather than d + 1 d{+}1 or 2 2 evaluations per estimated gradient. Existing averaging analyses of bounded ES concern deterministic ODEs; we extend the analysis to Itô SDEs.

3.2 The finite-step algorithm and practical guidance
sections.text: Algorithm 1 is the procedure used in all experiments. The methods for choosing ES gain k k , amplitude α \alpha , and frequencies ω i \omega_{i} are studied in more detail in Appendix C and D . Any pairwise-distinct positive constants satisfy Assumption 2 ; we use r i r_{i} evenly spaced (or i.i.d. uniform) in [ 1 , N ] [1,N] with modest N ∈ [ 1.75 , 2 ] N\in[1.75,2] . Euler-Maruyama must resolve the fastest dither: we use ω ​ r max ​ Δ ​ t ≤ 2 ​ π / 10 \omega r_{\max}\,\Delta t\leq 2\pi/10 so that at least 10 10 steps are required per fastest dither period. The product k ​ α k\alpha sets the strength of the emergent drift (Eq. 6 ) and the temperature of the averaged law ( ρ ∞ ∝ e − k ​ α ​ ℰ θ \rho_{\infty}\propto e^{-k\alpha\mathcal{E}_{\theta}} in (I λ )). Furthermore, if J J is changing slowly, we see from Eq. 5 that components will oscillate with amplitude proportional to α / ω i \sqrt{\alpha/\omega_{i}} , therefore in practice once ω i \omega_{i} is fixed, α \alpha is slowly increased until the dither is big enough to produce a good signal in the cost function and then k k is slowly increased until a reasonable rate of convergence is achieved. Excessive gain k ​ α k\alpha at any finite ω \omega can destabilize the ES dynamics.

sections.heading: 3.4 Latent-space sampling
sections.text: Applied in the latent space of a pretrained encoder–decoder ( E , D ) (E,D) , ES sampling becomes practical. Given an energy or log-density on latent codes 𝐳 ∈ ℝ d z \mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}} , d z ≪ d d_{z}\ll d , run Eq. ( 8 ) or Eq. ( 10 ) on 𝐳 \mathbf{z} and decode 𝐱 ^ = D ⁡ ( 𝐳 ) \hat{\mathbf{x}}=D(\mathbf{z}) . Three points: (i) d z d_{z} is small ( 3 3 – 512 512 in our experiments), so the frequency-gap constraint of Sec. 3.2 is mild and moderate ω \omega suffices; (ii) the decoder is used strictly as a black box—relevant when D D is frozen, exported, or quantized; (iii) latent diffusion ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) and latent EBMs are the dominant deployment pattern, so this is the natural setting. The geometry of the latent energy landscape governs whether ES (or any local sampler) succeeds there.

sections.heading: 3.5 CelebA-HQ tracking statistics and derivative-free benchmark
sections.text: Figure 2: Latent-space tracking from 1D RGB projections of time-varying images. For tracking time-varying CELEB-HQ images, the setup is shown in Figure 2 . sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: In this work, generative AI tools were used to proof-read the paper, to find typos or mathematical errors, for polishing the writing, and for discussion, suggestions, and collaboration on some of the mathematical results. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work. We checked LLM-suggested references through a manual literature survey. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: For all of the theoretical results, clear explanations of any assumptions and complete proofs of the claims are included in the appendix. For the proposed algorithm a clear explanation of exactly how it is applied has been provided. A complete description of data processing steps has also been provided.

( 77 ) with Δ ​ t = 2 ​ π / ( c ​ N ​ ω ) \Delta t=2\pi/(cN\omega) looks self-similar in ω \omega : the fastest dither always takes c c steps per oscillation and the slowest c ​ N cN . The substitution τ = ω ​ t \tau=\omega t (with the Brownian scaling d w ( t ) = ω − 1 / 2 d W ( τ ) dw(t)=\omega^{-1/2}dW(\tau) ) makes this precise and shows what does change: d x i = g α ​ r i ω cos ( r i τ + k ℰ ) d τ + g σ ω − 1 / 2 d W i ( τ ) . dx_{i}\;=\;g\sqrt{\tfrac{\alpha r_{i}}{\omega}}\,\cos\!\big(r_{i}\tau+k\mathcal{E}\big)\,d\tau\;+\;g\,\sigma\,\omega^{-1/2}\,dW_{i}(\tau). (80) On this fast clock the dither frequencies are the fixed ratios r i r_{i} and the Euler grid Δ ​ τ = 2 ​ π / ( c ​ N ) \Delta\tau=2\pi/(cN) is ω \omega -independent, but every term that moves the state carries ω − 1 / 2 \omega^{-1/2} : per dither period the state moves only O ( ω − 1 / 2 ) O(\omega^{-1/2}) , so the phase k ​ ℰ ​ ( 𝐱 ) k\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x}) is frozen to that order over each oscillation (the working condition of averaging, and the origin of the ω − 1 / 2 \omega^{-1/2} rate), while each step covers only 2 ​ π / ( c ​ N ​ ω ) 2\pi/(cN\omega) of slow time (the origin of the linear-in- ω \omega cost). ω \omega is thus the exchange rate between the clocks: the number of dither oscillations per unit of the averaged dynamics’ own timescale.

sections.heading: Beats and the gap criterion.
sections.text: Expanding the coordinate ripples (cf. the warm-up of A.2 ) into the phase, the drift of coordinate n n contains products of its dither with every coordinate’s ripple; by the product formulas these oscillate at the sum frequencies ( r n + r i ) ​ ω (r_{n}{+}r_{i})\omega (always fast) and the beat frequencies Δ n ​ i = ω ​ | r n − r i | \Delta_{ni}=\omega|r_{n}-r_{i}| , of which the smallest, for evenly spaced ratios, is Δ min = ( N − 1 ) ​ ω d − 1 . \Delta_{\min}\;=\;\frac{(N-1)\,\omega}{d-1}. (81) The resonant term i = n i=n (zero beat frequency) is the emergent gradient; every other term is an oscillatory integral ∫ 0 T A ⁡ ( t ) ​ cos ⁡ ( Δ ​ t ) ​ 𝑑 t \int_{0}^{T}A(t)\cos(\Delta t)\,dt with slowly varying envelope, bounded after one integration by parts by ( 2 ​ ‖ A ‖ ∞ + T ​ ‖ A ˙ ‖ ∞ ) / Δ (2\|A\|_{\infty}+T\|\dot{A}\|_{\infty})/\Delta : it is negligible precisely when the beat completes many cycles per unit of the slow timescale. Empirically “many” is a factor of order ten, giving the finite- ω \omega threshold Δ min ≳ O ( 10 ) ⟺ ω ∗ ( d ) ≈ O ​ ( 10 ) ​ ( d − 1 ) N − 1 , \Delta_{\min}\;\gtrsim\;O(10)\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\omega^{\ast}(d)\;\approx\;\frac{O(10)\,(d-1)}{N-1}, (82) with the constant measured below to be 5 5 – 15 15 . This converts the existence statement of Theorem 1 into a design formula: linear in d d , controlled by the band spread.

sections.heading: Why widening the band does not help.
sections.text: Resolving the fastest dither forces Δ ​ t = 2 ​ π / ( c ​ N ​ ω ) \Delta t=2\pi/(cN\omega) , so the evaluation cost per unit slow time is c ​ N ​ ω / 2 ​ π = c ​ ω max / 2 ​ π cN\omega/2\pi=c\,\omega_{\max}/2\pi — set by the top of the band ω max = N ​ ω \omega_{\max}=N\omega regardless of how it is split. At fixed ω max \omega_{\max} , widening N N buys relative minimum gap ( N − 1 ) / N (N{-}1)/N , which saturates immediately (already 0.67 0.67 at N = 3 N=3 ), while the slowest coordinates’ own averaging error remains at ( ω max / N ) − 1 / 2 (\omega_{\max}/N)^{-1/2} and the cross-term prefactors ω i / ω n ≤ N \sqrt{\omega_{i}/\omega_{n}}\leq\sqrt{N} grow. We therefore fix a modest band ( N ∈ [ 1.75 , 2 ] N\in[1.75,2] ) and scale the base frequency; the dimension cost is then intrinsic: reaching the asymptotic regime at dimension d d requires ω max = Ω ⁡ ( d ) \omega_{\max}=\Omega(d) and hence Ω ⁡ ( d ) \Omega(d) evaluations per unit slow time — the quantitative basis for the latent-space scoping of Sec. 3.2 .

sections.heading: Robustness checks.
sections.text: (i) Frequency-grid randomization. The evenly spaced grid is an arithmetic progression and therefore carries exact higher-order sum resonances ( r i + r k = 2 ​ r j r_{i}+r_{k}=2r_{j} for every consecutive triple). Jittering each ratio by up to 20 % 20\% of the grid spacing (destroying the exact resonances while keeping the gap scale; minimum gap 0.035 0.035 vs. 0.050 0.050 ) reproduces the linspace errors to within 2 % 2\% at every ω \omega and the local slopes to ± 0.02 \pm 0.02 (checked at d = 16 d=16 , σ = 0 \sigma=0 , c = 20 c=20 ; ω ∈ { 31.6,100,316 , 1000 } \omega\in\{31.6,100,316,1000\} : errors 3.62 / 1.68 / 0.616 / 0.245 3.62/1.68/0.616/0.245 vs. 3.60 / 1.71 / 0.621 / 0.251 3.60/1.71/0.621/0.251 , local slopes − 0.67 / − 0.87 / − 0.80 -0.67/-0.87/-0.80 vs. − 0.65 / − 0.88 / − 0.79 -0.65/-0.88/-0.79 ; 2 2 seeds, 64 64 chains). Grid design is thus not the origin of the low-noise steepening, and the practical recommendation “evenly spaced or i.i.d. ratios, fixed once” carries a data point. (ii) Floating point. The largest dither phase in these sweeps is ω max ​ T ≤ 2 × 10 5 \omega_{\max}T\leq 2\times 10^{5} radians, resolved by double precision to ∼ 10 − 11 \sim 10^{-11} radians, and the measured differences 𝐱 − 𝐱 ¯ \mathbf{x}-\bar{\mathbf{x}} are O ⁡ ( 10 − 1 ) O(10^{-1}) against states O ⁡ ( 1 ) O(1) : no cancellation is involved. Together with the 10 × 10\times step-refinement invariance of D.2 , the transition structure documented here is a property of the continuous-time coupled system, not of its implementation.

sections.text: Table 12 : the physical settling time is independent of ω \omega (all fitted slopes ≤ + 0.08 \leq+0.08 over two decades) and coincides with the averaged system’s own settling time (ratio 0.99 0.99 – 1.01 1.01 ) for every ( d , σ ) (d,\sigma) — convergence speed is governed by the averaged dynamics, an independent verification of Theorem 1 in a different observable than the trajectory error. Correspondingly the evaluation count to settle grows linearly in ω \omega (slopes + 1.01 +1.01 to + 1.08 +1.08 ). Combining the two measured laws with the rate of D.2 gives the efficiency scaling quoted in Sec. 3.2 : accuracy ∼ \sim (evaluations) -1/2 . sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: The comparison is designed around two symmetries identified during pilot experiments. Equal effective sample size: metrics are computed on the final states of 1024 1024 chains for every method — no trajectory pooling, whose effective sample size depends on each method’s decorrelation time. The finite-sample floor of the metric (sliced- W 2 W_{2} between an independent 1024 1024 -sample draw of the target and the reference set; 0.245 0.245 at d = 2 d{=}2 , 0.110 0.110 at d = 10 d{=}10 ) is reported, and entries within ∼ 15 % \sim\!15\% of it are marked unresolved. Symmetric tuning: every method’s hyperparameters are chosen by an identical pilot on a held-out seed (seed 0 0 ; evaluation uses seeds 1 1 – 5 5 ): step size h ∈ { 3 × 10 − 3 , 10 − 2 , 3 × 10 − 2 , 10 − 1 } h\in\{3{\times}10^{-3},10^{-2},3{\times}10^{-2},10^{-1}\} for the Langevin samplers, smoothing radius ν ∈ { 10 − 3 , 10 − 2 , 10 − 1 } \nu\in\{10^{-3},10^{-2},10^{-1}\} for the zeroth-order and finite-difference baselines, and the time/frequency split T ∈ { 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } T\in\{2,4,8,16,32\} (with ω = 2 ​ π ​ NFE / ( c ⋅ 1.75 ​ T ) \omega=2\pi\,\mathrm{NFE}/(c\cdot 1.75\,T) implied by the budget, c = 10 c=10 , and ω \omega constrained above the measured threshold) for ES. All methods target p p of Eq. ( 76 ); the ES rows use g = 2 g=\sqrt{2} , σ = 1 \sigma=1 , so that the averaged dynamics are the standard-speed Langevin diffusion.

sections.heading: Methods and per-step evaluation accounting.
Findings.
sections.text: ES is statistically indistinguishable from the tuned exact-gradient oracles in all four settings, at one evaluation per step; it resolves ahead of both derivative-free baselines at d = 2 d{=}2 , NFE = 2 × 10 3 \mathrm{NFE}{=}2{\times}10^{3} ; and the one clearly resolved deficit in the table is FD-ULA at d = 10 d{=}10 , 2 × 10 3 2{\times}10^{3} , whose d + 1 d{+}1 evaluations per step leave only NFE / 11 \mathrm{NFE}/11 steps and show as incomplete burn-in (mean final energy 20.4 20.4 vs. ≈ 15.7 \approx 15.7 for all other methods). We state the scope plainly: a smooth, low-dimensional testbed with every sampler tuned — the table supports parity at matched budget, not superiority.

sections.heading:
D.6 The mode-seeking configuration: a fixed-target benchmark against
derivative-free optimizers under measurement noise
sections.text: The comparison of D.5 evaluates the sampling configuration ( σ = 1 \sigma=1 : the averaged dynamics are the Langevin diffusion and the metric is distributional). This subsection evaluates the complementary mode-seeking configuration: the diffusion is taken to (numerically) zero, so that by the tempering corollary (Corollary 3 , stationary law ∝ p k ​ α / σ 2 \propto p^{\,k\alpha/\sigma^{2}} ) the averaged dynamics degenerate to the gradient flow 𝐱 ¯ ˙ = − k ​ α 2 ∇ ℰ ( 𝐱 ¯ ) \dot{\bar{\mathbf{x}}}=-\tfrac{k\alpha}{2}\nabla\mathcal{E}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) and the algorithm is being used as a derivative-free optimizer of the energy ℰ = − log ⁡ p \mathcal{E}=-\log p . This is the operating mode relevant to the tracking experiments, where the objective is to sit on the moving minimizer rather than to cover the posterior, and it is the mode in which the noise-robustness claim of Sec. 3.2 (“measurement noise on J J enters only through the dither phase”) can be tested quantitatively. The benchmark below therefore answers three questions on the testbed Eq. ( 76 ): (i) at matched total evaluation budgets, how does ES compare with the standard derivative-free optimization baselines — simultaneous-perturbation stochastic approximation (SPSA) ( Spall, 1992 ) , Gaussian-smoothing (GS) zeroth-order (ZO) gradient estimates ( Nesterov & Spokoiny, 2017 ; Ghadimi & Lan, 2013 ; Duchi et al., 2015 ; Salimans et al., 2017 ) , coordinate-wise finite differences (FD) ( Kiefer & Wolfowitz, 1952 ) , and adaptive random search ( Rechenberg, 1973 ) — when every evaluation of ℰ \mathcal{E} is corrupted by i.i.d. (independent and identically distributed) measurement noise; (ii) why ES behaves as it does under noise, via a derived and validated error-floor law; and (iii) what fraction of each method’s residual error is recoverable by cost-free iterate averaging, which isolates the coherent (dither-ripple) character of the ES residual.

sections.heading: Why a fixed-target protocol.
sections.text: Distributional metrics cannot score this regime: for the temperature-one target, the stationary energy gap is χ 2 \chi^{2} -distributed to excellent accuracy (the modes are ≥ 6 \geq 6 component widths apart), so a perfect sampler has 𝔼 ​ Δ ​ ℰ = d / 2 \mathbb{E}\,\Delta\mathcal{E}=d/2 by equipartition and essentially never enters a fixed energy ball — e.g. ℙ ⁡ ( Δ ​ ℰ < 1 2 ) = ℙ ⁡ ( χ 16 2 < 1 ) ≈ 6 × 10 − 8 \mathbb{P}(\Delta\mathcal{E}<\tfrac{1}{2})=\mathbb{P}(\chi^{2}_{16}<1)\approx 6\times 10^{-8} at d = 16 d=16 . Optimizers and samplers must therefore be benchmarked on different axes, and here we adopt the fixed-target (hitting-time) methodology standard in black-box optimization ( Hansen et al., 2021 ) : fix an accuracy target, record when each chain first reaches it, and report quantiles of the hitting-time distribution. The Langevin samplers of D.5 are correspondingly excluded from this table by construction, not by defeat.

sections.heading: Success criterion, dwell, and hitting times.
sections.text: With ℰ ⋆ = min m ⁡ ℰ ⁡ ( 𝝁 m ) \mathcal{E}^{\star}=\min_{m}\mathcal{E}(\bm{\mu}_{m}) (all four modes are equivalent), define the energy gap Δ ℰ ( 𝐱 ) = ℰ ( 𝐱 ) − ℰ ⋆ , Δ ℰ ( 𝐱 ) ≈ 1 2 ∥ 𝐱 − 𝝁 m ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) ∥ 2 near a mode , \Delta\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x})\;=\;\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x})-\mathcal{E}^{\star},\qquad\Delta\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x})\;\approx\;\tfrac{1}{2}\,\|\mathbf{x}-\bm{\mu}_{m(\mathbf{x})}\|^{2}\ \ \text{near a mode}, (83) so the target Δ ​ ℰ < ε \Delta\mathcal{E}<\varepsilon with ε = 1 2 \varepsilon=\tfrac{1}{2} is a ball of radius ≈ 2 ​ ε = 1 \approx\sqrt{2\varepsilon}=1 (one component width) around some mode, in every dimension. Let e e count the noisy oracle evaluations a method has consumed for a given chain (its only clock), and let 𝐱 ⁡ ( e ) \mathbf{x}(e) be that chain’s state, piecewise constant between the method’s updates. The per-chain hitting time is the first entry into a visit that persists , τ = min { e : Δ ℰ ( 𝐱 ( e ′ ) ) < ε for all e ′ ∈ [ e , e + D ] } , D = 20 evaluations , \tau\;=\;\min\Big\{\,e\;:\;\Delta\mathcal{E}\big(\mathbf{x}(e^{\prime})\big)<\varepsilon\ \ \text{for all}\ e^{\prime}\in[e,\,e+D]\,\Big\},\qquad D=20\ \text{evaluations}, (84) where the dwell requirement D D disqualifies transits in which a large dither excursion merely slices through the ball without settling (without it, hitting times can be gamed by amplitude). We report the success rate ℙ ⁡ ( τ ≤ B ) \mathbb{P}(\tau\leq B) over chains at the total per-chain budget B B , and the median hitting time E 50 E_{50} (the empirical 50 % 50\% quantile of τ \tau , in evaluations), quoting E 50 E_{50} only when at least half the chains succeed. Scoring uses the exact ℰ \mathcal{E} — available because the testbed is synthetic — and is not charged to any budget; the methods themselves never see it.

sections.text: Every method interacts with the energy only through the corrupted oracle ℰ ^ ​ ( 𝐱 ) = ℰ ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) + σ J ​ n , n ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) ​ i.i.d. per evaluation and per chain , \widehat{\mathcal{E}}(\mathbf{x})\;=\;\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x})+\sigma_{J}\,n,\qquad n\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\ \text{i.i.d.\ per evaluation and per chain}, (85) at noise levels σ J ∈ { 0.03 , 0.1 , 0.3 , 1.0 } \sigma_{J}\in\{0.03,\,0.1,\,0.3,\,1.0\} ; for reference, the initial gaps are Δ ​ ℰ ≈ 6 ​ d \Delta\mathcal{E}\approx 6d and the target is ε = 1 2 \varepsilon=\tfrac{1}{2} , so a single read at σ J = 0.1 \sigma_{J}=0.1 already carries noise equal to 20 % 20\% of the target resolution. This is the synthetic stand-in for a mini-batch or measurement-limited evaluation of a model’s energy.

sections.heading: Readout: last iterate vs. iterate averaging.
sections.text: Under a noisy oracle, scoring the final iterate of a stochastic trajectory is a high-variance convention; the standard remedy in stochastic approximation is Polyak–Ruppert iterate averaging ( Ruppert, 1988 ; Polyak & Juditsky, 1992 ) , whose deep-learning analogue is weight averaging ( Izmailov et al., 2018 ) . We therefore maintain, purely as a readout , an exponential moving average (EMA) in evaluation time, 𝐱 ¯ ← 𝐱 ¯ + λ ⁡ ( 𝐱 − 𝐱 ¯ ) , λ = min ⁡ ( 1 , Δ ​ e / τ f ) , τ f = 300 ​ evaluations , \bar{\mathbf{x}}\;\leftarrow\;\bar{\mathbf{x}}+\lambda\,(\mathbf{x}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}),\qquad\lambda=\min(1,\,\Delta e/\tau_{\mathrm{f}}),\qquad\tau_{\mathrm{f}}=300\ \text{evaluations}, (86) updated whenever the method updates ( Δ ​ e \Delta e = evaluations since the last update), and score Δ ​ ℰ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ ) \Delta\mathcal{E}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) . Three properties keep this fair: it is applied identically to every method; it costs zero evaluations (it reuses the trajectory already paid for); and it is feedback-free ( 𝐱 ¯ \bar{\mathbf{x}} never enters any method’s dynamics). Its one side effect is a warm-up lag: the average retains weight ≈ e − ( B − e conv ) / τ f \approx e^{-(B-e_{\mathrm{conv}})/\tau_{\mathrm{f}}} on pre-convergence states, so all EMA hitting times carry a common offset of order τ f ​ ln ⁡ ( Δ ​ ℰ 0 / ε ) \tau_{\mathrm{f}}\ln(\Delta\mathcal{E}_{0}/\varepsilon) , and a method that converges only near the end of its budget can show a larger EMA error than raw error. The clean-gradient oracle row below, which converges in ≤ 40 \leq 40 updates, measures this lag directly ( E 50 = 514 E_{50}=514 – 1211 1211 across d d ) and serves as the ruler; entries dominated by warm-up rather than by an error floor are marked † \dagger .

sections.text: The per-chain budget is identical for every method: B = 2000 B=2000 evaluations for d ≤ 64 d\leq 64 , 4000 4000 at d = 128 d=128 , 8000 8000 at d = 256 d=256 . Headline tables are mean ± \pm sd (standard deviation) over 5 5 replicates of 500 500 chains; a replicate re-draws the initialization, every method’s internal randomness, and the oracle noise stream, while within a replicate all methods share the same initialization and the same noise stream (common random numbers, so method-to-method comparisons are paired). Total evaluations is the fair currency for ES specifically because its evaluations are inherently sequential (each step’s evaluation feeds the next state), whereas the 2 ​ m 2m probes of ZO-GD, the 2 ​ d 2d of FD, and the 2 2 of SPSA are embarrassingly parallel across evaluators; wall-clock comparisons on parallel hardware would favor the batched estimators, and we say so rather than hide it. The converse structural advantage of the one-evaluation-per-step design — every coordinate updates after every single measurement, with no staleness window — is exercised by the time-varying benchmarks of D.7 , not by this static one. sections.heading:
Findings at low and moderate noise
(Tables 16 – 17 ).
sections.text: Tuned SPSA is the fastest derivative-free method at every dimension, as its query-model optimality leads one to expect; we state that plainly. The ES result is of a different kind: it reaches the target at every d ≤ 128 d\leq 128 at both noise levels (quadrature variant: success ≥ 97.4 % \geq 97.4\% everywhere), with E 50 E_{50} within 1.1 1.1 – 1.5 × 1.5\times of SPSA’s ( 1.10 1.10 – 1.43 × 1.43\times for the quadrature variant across d = 4 d=4 – 128 128 ), while operating under the strictly sequential one-evaluation-per-step constraint that is the point of the design. Every other baseline breaks somewhere in this range: cached-incumbent random search noise-locks (its stored incumbent value is a lucky order statistic that fresh proposals cannot beat ( Arnold & Beyer, 2002 ) ) already at ( d , σ J ) = ( 32 , 0.03 ) (d,\sigma_{J})=(32,0.03) ; the re-evaluating repair pays 2 × 2\times per step and still fails for d ≥ 64 d\geq 64 , because accepting on noisy comparisons turns the elitist walk into a diffusion whose drift vanishes once the per-step improvement falls below the 2 ​ σ J \sqrt{2}\,\sigma_{J} comparison noise; FD-GD is budget-starved by its 2 ​ d 2d -evaluation tax ( ≤ 15 \leq 15 updates at d ≥ 64 d\geq 64 ) on top of its noise amplification; and ZO-GD with m = 10 m=10 is squeezed by budget quantization ( ⌊ B / 20 ⌋ \lfloor B/20\rfloor updates — visible as the 74 74 – 79 % 79\% success at d = 64 d=64 , where it affords only 100 100 updates). The quadrature variant is never worse than the base variant and is consistently better in the tails (e.g. 99.1 99.1 vs. 95.9 % 95.9\% at ( 64 , 0.03 ) (64,0.03) ; 78.0 78.0 vs. 47.7 % 47.7\% at ( 256 , 0.03 ) (256,0.03) ), consistent with its elimination of the nearest-beat cross terms at fixed band. At d = 256 d=256 the current configuration reaches its measured boundary: the dither-envelope floor derived below ( ≈ 0.0028 ​ d = 0.72 \approx 0.0028\,d=0.72 at d = 256 d=256 ) exceeds ε \varepsilon under the raw readout, the gain schedule Eq. ( 89 ) crosses the finite-gain ceiling discussed below, and E 50 = 7506 E_{50}=7506 presses the B = 8000 B=8000 budget — three compounding effects, all of which the frequency-scaling prescription of D.3 (raise ω \omega with d d ) is designed to relieve; we report the boundary rather than re-tune past it.

sections.heading:
The ES residual is coherent
(Table 18 ).
sections.text: The readout study answers a question the headline tables cannot: what kind of error does each method leave behind? Averaging the trajectory can only remove zero-mean scatter about the right place; it does nothing for a chain that never arrived. The table shows exactly this taxonomy. The noise-locked random search is untouched by the filter ( 0.575 → 0.572 0.575\to 0.572 ): its error is dynamical, and the experiment thereby also certifies that the noise is not being filtered before the optimizers — if it were, every method would revert to its clean numbers. SPSA improves 4.6 × 4.6\times at σ J = 0.03 \sigma_{J}=0.03 (its residual is a weakly correlated stochastic wander). ES improves 7.5 × 7.5\times (base) and 12.0 × 12.0\times (quadrature, 0.108 → 0.009 0.108\to 0.009 ): its residual is dominated by the deterministic dither ripple — a zero-mean, phase-locked oscillation of known period ( 5 5 – 9 9 steps here) that any window much longer than a beat cancels coherently. This is the same structure exploited by a lock-in amplifier’s output low-pass filter ( Scofield, 1994 ) : the dithered phase demodulation of Sec. 3.2 is the mixer, and Eq. ( 86 ) is the missing output stage. The practical consequence is that the correct deployment of the mode-seeking configuration reports the averaged iterate, at zero additional evaluations — which is also what converts the d = 128 d=128 column of Table 17 from a raw-readout floor sitting near ε \varepsilon into a 97 97 – 100 % 100\% success rate.

sections.heading: Scope.
sections.text: We state the limits of this benchmark plainly, as in D.5 . The testbed is smooth with near-quadratic, unit-curvature basins, which grants the smoothing baselines their free noise-scaled probes and makes tuned SPSA close to its query-model optimum; none of the results here claim ES superiority on clean, smooth objectives, and the parallelism asymmetry noted in the accounting paragraph favors the batched estimators on parallel hardware. What the benchmark does establish, with five-seed error bars: (i) a strictly sequential, one-evaluation-per-step method reaches the fixed target at every d ≤ 128 d\leq 128 under evaluation noise, within 1.1 1.1 – 1.5 × 1.5\times the evaluation cost of the strongest (noise-tuned, parallelizable) baseline, where every other sequential-friendly baseline fails; (ii) the noise-robustness mechanism claimed in Sec. 3.2 is quantitative — rates within 8 8 – 13 % 13\% of noiseless up to k ​ σ J ≈ 0.2 k\sigma_{J}\approx 0.2 , with the residual cost captured by the derived floor law Eq. ( 91 ) to a few percent over an order of magnitude in d d and in σ J 2 \sigma_{J}^{2} ; and (iii) the ES residual is coherent rather than stochastic, so a zero-cost averaged readout recovers up to 12 × 12\times accuracy — the lock-in signature that distinguishes the dither mechanism from stochastic smoothing.

sections.heading: D.7 CelebA-HQ: steady-state lag and paired comparison
sections.text: This appendix supplements the CelebA-HQ tracking study of Sec. 3.5 : the first paragraph reads the checkpoint-by-checkpoint NMSE of Table 2 (target drift vs. bounded ES) as a quantitative measurement of the tracking mechanism, and the second returns to the matched-budget benchmark of Table 4 to explain the ranking it reports.

sections.heading: Steady-state-lag signature.
sections.text: The checkpoint increments expose the tracking mechanism quantitatively. Between consecutive checkpoints the target’s NMSE advances by Δ drift = .053 , .068 , .075 , .084 , .095 , .110 \Delta_{\mathrm{drift}}=.053,.068,.075,.084,.095,.110 (the drift accelerates), while the tracker’s residual advances by Δ ES = .009 , .010 , .011 , .012 , .015 , .016 \Delta_{\mathrm{ES}}=.009,.010,.011,.012,.015,.016 ; the ratio Δ ES / Δ drift = .170 , .147 , .147 , .143 , .158 , .145 \Delta_{\mathrm{ES}}/\Delta_{\mathrm{drift}}=.170,.147,.147,.143,.158,.145 is constant at 0.152 ± 0.010 0.152\pm 0.010 across all six intervals, after a standing-start first checkpoint at level ratio 0.40 0.40 . A constant incremental ratio is the signature of steady-state lag tracking: the residual is proportional to the target’s local speed with a fixed effective response time, the stochastic analogue of the deterministic ES tracking bounds of ( Scheinker & Scheinker, 2016 ) , and it implies the 6 × 6\times headline reduction is not a plateau but improves whenever the target moves more slowly. Tuning improves the baselines considerably, SPSA most of all, yet bounded ES remains the strongest forward-only method: 1.8 × 1.8\times lower final NMSE than best-tuned SPSA, 3.5 × 3.5\times lower than FD, 15 × 15\times lower than GS-ES, and within 1.7 × 1.7\times of the exact-gradient oracle. Because all methods are run on the same 219 219 pairs and seeds, the comparison is paired: bounded ES achieves the lowest final NMSE among the four forward-only methods on 100 % 100\% of the 219 219 pairs — 219 / 219 219/219 head-to-head wins against each of SPSA, FD, and GS-ES — while outperforming even the exact-gradient oracle on ≈ 9 % \approx 9\% of pairs (exact instantaneous gradients are not optimal for a moving target: Adam’s momentum can overshoot or lag the target’s turns, and on those pairs the ES trajectory ends closer). The ranking is explained by the update rate against a moving target rather than by per-estimate variance. Bounded ES commits an update after every single measurement ( 8192 8192 updates); SPSA after every 2 2 ( 4096 4096 ); GS-ES only after 2 ​ m 2m consecutive measurements — its antithetic pairs are evaluated at different times against a moving target, so temporal drift contaminates the spatial differences, and the tuned m m trades estimator variance against staleness with no good operating point at this drift rate: its final NMSE ( 1.17 1.17 ) exceeds the targets’ own final drift ( ≈ 0.51 \approx 0.51 , Table 2 ), i.e., it ends farther from the target than the untouched initial image. Beyond the raw evaluation-count tax (cf. Table 15 ), coordinate FD suffers the structural staleness penalty in its purest form: with d = 256 d=256 parameters, central differences must hold the state essentially fixed for 512 512 measurements to assemble one gradient estimate, so its entire budget purchases 16 16 steps, each applying the gradient of a target that no longer exists — the estimate answers a question the system is no longer asking — whereas ES updates every coordinate after every single measurement.

sections.text: Latents are standardized per channel to zero mean and standard deviation 0.5 0.5 with the statistics of 45,000 45{,}000 training latents ( 5,000 5{,}000 are held out for validation). On the 10,000 10{,}000 test images the VAE reconstructs with PSNR = 28.2 =28.2 dB, SSIM = 0.90 =0.90 Wang et al. (2004) and a mean absolute error of 0.060 0.060 on the [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] pixel scale, so the decoder’s own reconstruction error is about 2.6 × 2.6\times smaller than the tracker’s final-frame error against the decoded targets reported below. Encoder and decoder use exponential-moving-average weights, and every image in the tracking study is a decoder output D θ ​ ( z ) D_{\theta}(z) , so the targets lie on the decoder’s image manifold by construction. The latent diffusion U-Net has 17.0 17.0 M parameters; base width 128 128 , two residual blocks per level, multi-head self-attention at every level and at bottleneck. Appendix F Dimension dependence of the finite-frequency threshold and
the evaluation cost of ES
sections.text: Theorem 1 is dimension-free in form : for every ( δ , ε , T ) (\delta,\varepsilon,T) there is a finite ω ∗ \omega^{*} , whatever the state dimension. All dependence on the dimension is compressed into ω ∗ ​ ( δ , ε , T ) \omega^{*}(\delta,\varepsilon,T) through the constant C R ′ C_{R}^{\prime} of Eq. ( 46 ), which silently sums the O ⁡ ( d 2 ) O(d^{2}) cross-coordinate oscillatory integrals of Step 2, and through the frequency gaps | r n − r i | |r_{n}-r_{i}| entering the constants of Lemma 1 . Read naively, the theory appears to work equally well in any dimension; in experiments the finite- ω \omega threshold grows linearly with d d (Eq. ( 82 ), Table 11 ). This appendix closes the gap between those two statements. We prove: (i) an explicit finite- ω \omega error bound whose constants carry the dimension polynomially, so that a sufficient threshold ω ∗ ​ ( d ) \omega^{*}(d) is polynomial in d d (Proposition 4 ); (ii) a matching-in- d d lower bound: for the evenly spaced frequency design there are C ∞ C^{\infty} targets for which no ω ≲ d / T \omega\lesssim d/T suffices, so ω ∗ ​ ( d ) = Ω ⁡ ( d / ( ( r max − 1 ) ​ T ) ) \omega^{*}(d)=\Omega\!\big(d/((r_{\max}-1)T)\big) (Proposition 6 ), the rigorous counterpart of the measured law Eq. ( 82 ); and (iii) the consequence the practitioner feels: combined with the step-resolution requirement of Algorithm 1 , the number of model evaluations needed to track the averaged dynamics grows at least linearly in d d , for every choice of the frequency band (Theorem 5 ). The averaged limit itself never sees the dimension; the entire cost is paid through the exchange rate ω \omega between the fast and slow clocks of Eq. ( 80 ). Throughout this appendix d d denotes the state dimension (the N N of Appendix A.1 ), and the frequency ratios are { r i } i = 1 d ⊂ [ 1 , r max ] \{r_{i}\}_{i=1}^{d}\subset[1,r_{\max}] ; to avoid a notation collision we write r max r_{\max} for the top of the band, denoted N N in Appendix D.3 . For the evenly spaced design, adjacent ratios differ by δ r = ( r max − 1 ) / ( d − 1 ) \delta_{r}=(r_{\max}-1)/(d-1) , so the smallest beat frequency is Δ min = ω ​ δ r \Delta_{\min}=\omega\delta_{r} as in Eq. ( 81 ).

sections.heading: F.1 Dimension-normalized setting

We prove that trajectories of the dithered Itô SDE converge to those of the target SDE, driven by the same Brownian motion, uniformly on compact time intervals in probability, by an averaging argument that extends bounded extremum seeking (ES) to Itô processes, with an explicit O ( ω − 1 / 2 ) O(\omega^{-1/2}) mean-square rate under global bounds. The approach is not confined to smooth targets: it extends to C 1 , 1 C^{1,1} energies with discontinuous curvature (without ellipticity requirement) and to Sobolev energies whose Hessians exist only off measure zero sets; for Lipschitz energies with gradient kinks the averaged limit remains well posed; the Krylov-Röckner integrability class is the boundary of provability. The approach provides a hard a priori bound on the per-step update rate and applies to explicitly time-varying targets on finite horizons. Gradient-free pixel-space sampling is not competitive with well-tuned backpropagation-based samplers at practical evaluation budgets; the regime where the approach offers an advantage is latent-space sampling when the model is a black box and the target drifts in time. We demonstrate latent-space tracking for time-varying images on CelebA-HQ ( 256 × 256 256{	imes}256 ) from limited 1D projection measurements and latent-space EBM sampling on CIFAR-10. 1 Introduction Modern generative models are trained, sampled, and conditioned primarily through gradients of large neural networks. Score-based diffusion ( Song et al., 2021 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song & Ermon, 2019 ) , latent diffusion ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023 ) , and energy-based models (EBMs) ( Du & Mordatch, 2019 ; Grathwohl et al., 2020 ; Du et al., 2021 ) all rely on gradients of a trained network: guidance or likelihood signals for diffusion and flow models, and the energy gradient itself for EBMs. When the model is available inside an automatic-differentiation framework this is efficient: a backward pass costs a small constant multiple of a forward pass. Our interest is in settings where even this is unavailable or insufficient. Three such regimes recur in practice. (i) : The quantity of interest is computed by a simulator ( Cranmer et al., 2020 ) , a black-box scoring function such as the round-trip self-consistency of a bidirectional diffusion rollout ( Scheinker, 2026 ) , a quantized or compiled inference engine, or a model served behind an API, so that only function values can be obtained ( Nesterov & Spokoiny, 2017 ) . (ii) : The target distribution drifts continuously, which is the operating condition of feedback-based generative reconstruction in scientific instruments, such as evolving microstructures in dynamic coherent diffraction imaging ( Scheinker & Pokharel, 2024 ) , time-varying particle accelerator beam diagnostics ( Scheinker et al., 2026 ; Scheinker, 2024 ) , and more broadly of streaming inverse problems in which each new measurement redefines the posterior. Restarting an MCMC chain at every measurement is wasteful, and running a single gradient-based chain against a drifting target has no tracking guarantee. (iii) : Sampling in the latent space of a pretrained encoder-decoder whose internals are frozen or otherwise outside the user’s autodiff graph, as in generative-prior inverse problems ( Bora et al., 2017 ) and latent-space molecular design ( Gómez-Bombarelli et al., 2018 ) .
